opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the biggest lesson for us has been that reliability doesn't come from the model getting smarter about a giant flat list of tools. It comes from structure around the model.

The first thing we do is avoid exposing everything at once. Once you get past a couple dozen tools, the descriptions start to blur together and the model begins picking the "close enough" one. So we group tools into a hierarchy: the agent first decides what kind of task it's in, and only then sees the small set of tools relevant to that context. That alone cuts down a lot of the wrong-tool errors.

The second thing is investing in the tool descriptions themselves, almost like writing documentation for a new teammate. Clear names, when to use it, when *not* to use it, and examples of inputs. A surprising amount of failure comes from two tools that sound similar but have subtly different contracts. If a human engineer would be confused reading the descriptions, the model will be too.

Third, we try to make tools forgiving and checkable. Strict schemas, validation on the arguments, and error messages written so the model can actually recover, saying what went wrong and what a correct call looks like, rather than just returning a stack trace. A lot of reliability is really about graceful recovery, not getting it perfect the first time.

And finally, evaluation. Every time we add tools, we rerun a set of realistic tasks and look at which tool got chosen, not just whether the final answer was right. Sometimes the agent stumbles into the right outcome through the wrong path, and that's a fragility you want to catch early.

So the short version: keep the choice set small at any moment, write tools for the reader, design for recovery, and measure the selection behavior directly as the toolbox grows.

r001.rationale: The response recommends grouping tools hierarchically and showing the agent a small relevant set, but does not describe assigning designated tool sets to sub-agents.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something we ran into pretty early, and I think the honest answer is that the naive approach breaks much sooner than people expect. When you have five tools, you can just dump all the descriptions into the context and the model does fine. Somewhere around twenty or thirty, you start seeing the model pick a plausible-sounding tool that isn't quite right, or hallucinate arguments, or get confused between two tools that overlap. And the failure modes are subtle, because the agent doesn't error out, it just does something slightly wrong and keeps going.

So the first thing we did was stop treating tool selection as a single flat decision. We organize tools hierarchically, almost like a file system. The agent first decides what category of thing it needs to do, and only then does it see the specific tools within that category, with their full schemas. That keeps the context at any given decision point small, and it also mirrors how a person would think about it. You don't scan every API you have access to, you think "I need to get data from somewhere" and then narrow down.

The second piece is retrieval over the tool descriptions themselves. We embed the tool documentation and, given the current subtask, we surface the handful of tools that are most likely relevant. That's a very simple idea but it works surprisingly well, and it means adding a new tool doesn't degrade performance on everything else.

The third thing, which I think is underrated, is investing in the tool interfaces rather than the agent. A lot of what looks like a reasoning failure is really an interface failure. If two tools have ambiguous names, or one takes a date string and another takes a timestamp, the model will get it wrong a certain percentage of the time no matter how good it is. So we spend real effort making tools orthogonal, giving them descriptive names, having them return structured, informative errors. When a call fails, the error message should tell the model what to do differently, not just say "invalid input."

And then we validate before execution. Arguments get checked against the schema, and if something's off, the model gets a chance to fix it before anything actually runs. That alone catches a huge fraction of the problems.

The thing I'd say overall is that reliability here is mostly an engineering problem, not a modeling problem. The model is capable enough. The question is whether you've set up the environment so that the right choice is the obvious one.

r001.rationale: The response recommends hierarchical tool categories and retrieval, but does not describe assigning designated tool sets to sub-agents.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that choosing a tool and using it correctly are two separate problems. As the tool set grows, you don’t necessarily want every agent to see every tool at every step. You want to narrow that choice based on the task, and then give the agent the context it needs to use the relevant tools well.

So one structure is a routing layer that identifies the kind of work needed, with more focused agents that each have access to a smaller set of tools. But that introduces another potential failure point: did you route the task correctly? You have to look at the whole chain, including whether the arguments were right and whether the tool’s output actually answered the question.

And I think explicit feedback is important. If a tool call fails, the agent needs a useful error signal and a bounded way to recover. Adding more agents alone doesn’t make tool use reliable; keeping their responsibilities clear and checking the results is what matters.

r001.rationale: The response recommends routing work to focused agents, each with access to a smaller set of relevant tools, as the tool set grows.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that tool selection and tool execution are two separate problems. As the number of tools grows, you don’t necessarily want every agent considering every tool at every step. You can organize tools around capabilities and give an agent access to the subset that’s relevant to its task.

But narrowing that choice is only part of reliability. You also need to check whether the arguments make sense, whether the tool actually succeeded, and whether its output supports the next step. An agent shouldn’t treat making a tool call as equivalent to accomplishing the task.

So I’d favor a fairly simple structure: clear responsibilities, limited tool access, and explicit checks at the boundaries. Then, as you add tools, you can evaluate whether failures come from choosing the wrong tool, using it incorrectly, or misinterpreting the result. That distinction helps you improve the system without just adding more agents.

r001.rationale: The response recommends giving an agent a relevant subset of tools, but does not clearly describe assigning designated tool sets to sub-agents.
